curriculum_source: CFA Program 2027 Level III, Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct (original study items)

reading.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

drills.los_text: explain the purpose of the Asset Manager Code and the benefits that may accrue to a firm that adopts the Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: Compared with the CFA Institute Code of Ethics and Standards of Professional Conduct, the Asset Manager Code is most accurately described as:

options.A: A voluntary firm-level code a manager may adopt even if not every employee is a CFA charterholder; individual members and candidates remain bound by the Standards whether or not the firm has adopted the Code.
options.B: A mandatory replacement for the individual Code and Standards at any shop that employs even one charterholder, so personal duties under the Standards lapse once the firm files its adoption notice with clients.
options.C: An annual individual attestation that each charterholder signs; the firm itself is never the adopting party, and clients look only to each employee's personal Standards file for process rules.

rationales.A: Correct. The Asset Manager Code is voluntary and binds the FIRM that adopts it. The Code and Standards continue to bind individual members and candidates regardless of the firm's adoption.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Adoption is not mandatory just because the firm employs charterholders, and it does not replace personal duties under the Standards.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The adopting party is the firm. Individual attestations are not how the Asset Manager Code is taken on.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — firm vs individual

questions.stem: A benefit that may accrue to a firm that adopts the Asset Manager Code is most likely:

options.A: A CFA Institute endorsement of the firm's composite returns, which the firm may then quote in RFPs as evidence that its track record has been certified by the Institute.
options.B: A documented ethical framework clients, consultants, and regulators can inspect, plus one internal standard for allocation, valuation, trading, and performance instead of desk-by-desk custom.
options.C: Automatic relief from Standard III(A) and Standard V(A) for every employee, because firm-level adoption is treated as a substitute for the individual Standards those employees already follow.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Adoption is not a performance claim and not a CFA Institute endorsement of the firm or its returns.
rationales.B: Correct. Benefits include a public, inspectable framework and internal consistency across the processes the six principles cover. It is a culture and process signal, not a return certificate.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Individual Standards still bind members and candidates. Firm adoption does not waive III(A) or V(A).

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — benefits of adoption

questions.stem: A marketing deck for a firm that has adopted the Asset Manager Code states that “CFA Institute has approved our returns.” Relative to the purpose of the Code, this claim is most likely:

options.A: Consistent, because adoption is the Institute's process for certifying composites once the firm names a compliance officer and files the Code with its regulator. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Consistent only for GIPS-verified firms; adoption of the Asset Manager Code is the Institute's endorsement route for shops that have not yet claimed GIPS compliance.
options.C: Inconsistent with the purpose of the Code. Adoption is not an endorsement, not a performance guarantee, and must not be marketed as Institute approval of the firm's results.

rationales.A: Incorrect. There is no Institute certification of returns attached to adopting the Code.
rationales.B: Incorrect. GIPS verification and Asset Manager Code adoption are separate. Neither is an Institute endorsement of returns.
rationales.C: Correct. The Code's purpose is a voluntary firm-level ethics framework. Marketing that implies CFA Institute certified the firm's returns violates that purpose (and the spirit of Standard VII(B)).

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — not an endorsement

questions.stem: A boutique has two CFA charterholders and eight other investment staff who are not members or candidates. The firm wants a single public ethics framework covering IPO allocation and private-asset valuation. The most appropriate statement is:

options.A: The firm can adopt the Asset Manager Code even though not every employee is a charterholder; the two charterholders remain personally bound by the Standards in any event.
options.B: The firm cannot adopt the Code until every investment employee becomes a member or candidate, because the Code only attaches through individual membership. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: The two charterholders' personal Standard III and V duties already cover firm-level IPO allocation and Level-3 valuation, so adopting a firm code would be redundant.

rationales.A: Correct. Adoption is a firm act, not a headcount of charterholders. Individual Standards still bind the two members; they do not by themselves write the firm's allocation and valuation manuals.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Non-charterholder staff do not block firm-level adoption. The Code is written for the manager as an organization.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Individual Standards do not fully specify firm processes such as IPO books and private-asset valuation policy — that is a reason the firm-level Code exists.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — who may adopt

questions.stem: Which vignette is most clearly in the Asset Manager Code's lane rather than only the individual Code and Standards?

options.A: One research analyst's working papers omit a source, raising a Standard V(C) recordkeeping issue that is confined to that analyst's files and does not describe a firm procedure.
options.B: How THE FIRM allocates an oversubscribed IPO across accounts, values a private holding, or writes the compliance manual that desks are required to follow. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: A candidate's weekend social-media post about exam content, which is a Standard VII(A) issue about the individual's conduct as a candidate, not a firm investment process. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Incorrect. A single analyst's research file is individual Standards territory (typically V(C)/I(C)), not the firm-level Code.
rationales.B: Correct. The discrimination is firm vs individual. Allocation, valuation policy, and the compliance manual are firm practices the Asset Manager Code is built to judge.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Candidate exam-discussion rules are Standard VII, not the Asset Manager Code.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — firm vs analyst vignette

questions.stem: The purpose of a public, firm-wide Asset Manager Code is most likely that:

options.A: Clients can observe every trade, valuation mark, and allocation in real time, so a published code is mainly a marketing brochure rather than a substitute for surveillance they already perform. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Regulators in every jurisdiction forbid a manager to operate without this specific Code, so adoption is the legal license to manage third-party assets rather than a voluntary ethics framework.
options.C: Clients cannot watch every trade, valuation, or allocation; a public firm-wide code is one place they can look for how the firm says it will handle loyalty, process, trading, risk, performance, and disclosure.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Clients generally cannot watch every decision. That opacity is why a public firm-level code has a purpose.
rationales.B: Incorrect. The Code is voluntary. Some regulators require a written code of ethics; this Code is a ready-made way to meet that expectation, not a universal license.
rationales.C: Correct. The Code exists because asset-management clients cannot monitor every internal decision. A published firm-wide commitment gives them a single framework to compare with actual procedures.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS a — why a public firm code

drills.los_text: explain the ethical and professional responsibilities required by the six General Principles of Conduct of the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: The six General Principles of Conduct of the Asset Manager Code, in the usual study order, are most likely:

options.A: Loyalty to Clients; Investment Process and Actions; Trading; Risk Management, Compliance, and Support; Performance and Valuation; Disclosures. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Professionalism; Integrity of Capital Markets; Duties to Clients; Duties to Employers; Investment Analysis; Conflicts of Interest — the individual Standards restated for firms.
options.C: Best execution; GIPS composites; personal-account pre-clearance; independent directors; custody; and cyber insurance, which together replace the six principles. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Six principles, in this order: Loyalty to Clients; Investment Process and Actions; Trading; Risk Management, Compliance, and Support; Performance and Valuation; Disclosures.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Those are the individual Standards I–VI, not the Asset Manager Code's six General Principles.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Those are controls that may support the principles; they are not the six principles themselves.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — six principles in order

questions.stem: Loyalty to Clients under the Asset Manager Code most likely requires the firm to:

options.A: Maximize the firm's proprietary-book profit whenever a client mandate is silent, because loyalty is owed first to the firm's shareholders and only residually to advisory clients.
options.B: Place client interests first, preserve confidentiality of client information, and refuse gifts or entertainment that reasonably could affect independence or compete with the client's interest.
options.C: Treat every client identically, including identical product mixes and share counts, because loyalty is defined as sameness of outcome across the book of accounts. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Loyalty is the firm's duty to the client relationship, not a residual after the proprietary book is served.
rationales.B: Correct. Principle 1 is client-first, confidentiality, and no consideration that could reasonably affect independence. It parallels — but does not replace — Standard III(A) for the individual.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Fair dealing is not identical treatment. Different mandates should receive different allocations.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Loyalty to Clients

questions.stem: Under the Trading principle, fair allocation of an oversubscribed IPO is most accurately described as:

options.A: Giving every account, including those that never buy IPOs, the same share count so that no client can claim to have been treated worse than another on a headcount basis.
options.B: Filling the firm's proprietary account and favored relationships first, then allocating residual shares pro rata to advisory clients who happen to still have cash. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Allocating trades and opportunities — including IPOs — fairly given each client's mandate, not by mechanical headcount and not by favoring the proprietary book or selected relationships.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Identical share counts across unlike accounts is often the violation. Fair dealing follows mandate, not headcount.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Personal or firm trades must not be placed ahead of client trades.
rationales.C: Correct. Trading requires best execution and fair allocation by mandate. Equal counts is not the same as fair allocation.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Trading / fair allocation

questions.stem: Risk Management, Compliance, and Support is most likely satisfied when the firm:

options.A: Maintains a compliance program with a named officer who has authority, identifies and manages portfolio and business risk, and provides the people and systems the principles actually require.
options.B: Prints “Chief Compliance Officer” on one trader's business card, with no budget, no halt authority, and no surveillance systems beyond the trading desk's own blotter.
options.C: Outsources all compliance judgment to the portfolio manager of each strategy, on the view that the people closest to the trades are best placed to police themselves. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Principle 4 is a real program: named officer with authority, risk identification, and resources. A title without budget is not a program.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A one-person title with no authority or systems fails Principle 4.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Self-policing by the trading desk is the opposite of an independent compliance function with halt authority.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — compliance program

questions.stem: Performance and Valuation under the Asset Manager Code most likely requires the firm to:

options.A: Present only currently live accounts and replace hard-to-value holdings with cost until a sale, so that reported results stay smooth and comparable across periods. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Present performance that is fair, accurate, timely, and complete, and use fair-market valuations with a documented policy — especially for illiquid holdings — without cherry-picking accounts, periods, or composites.
options.C: Use the last-round private-company price indefinitely after a material down round, because a documented mark would be more subjective than leaving cost on the books.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Dropping terminated accounts and parking illiquid names at cost is cherry-picking / stale valuation, not complete performance.
rationales.B: Correct. Principle 5 is fair, accurate, timely, complete performance and documented fair-market valuation, particularly for Level-3 assets.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Stale last-round cost after a material event is a valuation failure, not conservatism.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Performance and Valuation

questions.stem: The Disclosures principle is most likely breached when the firm:

options.A: Sends clients a timely, accurate description of a new performance-fee tier, the conflict it creates, and the date the change takes effect, and keeps a file of what was sent.
options.B: Describes risks, fees, and process in the IPS and ADV, then separately emails material changes when the investment process or fee schedule actually changes. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Stays silent about a conflict because the underlying trade was allocated by a written policy the firm considers fair; silence about the conflict is still a disclosure failure.

rationales.A: Incorrect. That is the kind of timely, complete communication Principle 6 requires.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Ongoing disclosure of material changes is consistent with the principle.
rationales.C: Correct. Principle 6 requires timely, accurate, complete communication about conflicts, fees, risks, and material changes. A fair trade does not excuse silence about the conflict.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS b — Disclosures

drills.los_text: determine whether an asset manager's practices and procedures are consistent with the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: A firm gives every client account 400 shares of an oversubscribed IPO, including an account whose mandate never buys IPOs. This practice is most likely:

options.A: Inconsistent with the Code. Fair allocation follows objectives, constraints, and mandate; equal share counts that pad non-IPO accounts are not fair dealing under Trading.
options.B: Consistent with the Code, because identical share counts prove that no account was favored and Loyalty to Clients is defined as sameness of outcome.
options.C: Outside the Code's scope, because IPO allocation is solely a Standard III(B) individual-member issue and cannot be judged as a firm practice. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Equal counts is not fair allocation. Accounts that do not participate in IPOs should not be padded; suitable accounts should not be shorted to make the headcount even.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Sameness of share count across unlike mandates is often the breach, not the cure.
rationales.C: Incorrect. This is a classic firm-practice item under the Asset Manager Code (Trading / fair allocation), even though an individual could also breach III(B).

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — equal-share IPO

questions.stem: A year after a material down round, a private holding still sits at last-round cost; there is no documented valuation policy. This practice is most likely:

options.A: Consistent with Performance and Valuation, because cost is more objective than a mark and leaving last-round cost avoids disputable fair-value estimates.
options.B: Inconsistent with Performance and Valuation. Illiquid holdings need a documented fair-value policy with timely review after material events, not stale cost.
options.C: A Loyalty issue only, because any stale mark is first a confidentiality failure toward the issuer rather than a performance-presentation problem. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Cost after a material event is not conservatism; it is an incomplete, stale valuation.
rationales.B: Correct. Map the action to Principle 5. A private holding at last-round cost a year after a down round, with no policy, is inconsistent with the Code.
rationales.C: Incorrect. The broken duty is valuation / performance presentation, not issuer confidentiality.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — stale private mark

questions.stem: The person titled compliance officer reports into the trading desk and cannot halt a trade. Relative to the Code this arrangement is most likely:

options.A: Consistent, provided the officer's title appears in the firm's ADV and marketing, because Principle 4 is satisfied by naming someone rather than by halt authority.
options.B: Consistent if the trading desk documents each override, because a reporting line into trading improves speed and therefore best execution under Principle 3.
options.C: Inconsistent with Risk Management, Compliance, and Support. A compliance program requires a named officer who has authority, not a title that cannot stop a trade.

rationales.A: Incorrect. A title without authority is not a program.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Reporting into the desk that must be policed undermines independence; speed is not a substitute for halt authority.
rationales.C: Correct. Principle 4 fails when compliance cannot restrict trading or escalate. Judge the procedure as described, not the org-chart label.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — CO without authority

questions.stem: Which firm practice is most likely consistent with the Asset Manager Code?

options.A: A written IPO/new-issue allocation policy applied by client mandate, with records retained, rather than a same-share-count rule across unlike accounts. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: A composite that drops terminated accounts and backfills a model return for the first six months of a new strategy so that the marketed track record stays continuous.
options.C: Employee trades in names on the restricted list filling before the client order in the same security, provided the employee ticket is smaller than the client's. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Written allocation by mandate with records is the consistent pattern. Equal counts, dropped accounts, and employee priority are classic inconsistencies.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Dropping terminated accounts and model backfill is incomplete / cherry-picked performance.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Personal trades must not be placed ahead of client trades, regardless of ticket size.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — consistent allocation policy

questions.stem: The firm's proprietary account is filled in a name before the client order in that name is complete. This practice is most likely:

options.A: Consistent with Trading so long as execution quality on the client remainder meets the firm's best-execution policy after the proprietary fill. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Inconsistent with Trading (and Loyalty). The firm must not place personal or proprietary trades ahead of client trades in the same name. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Outside the Code, because proprietary-book timing is a capital-structure choice for the management company and is not a client-facing procedure.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Best execution on the leftover does not cure front-running the client.
rationales.B: Correct. Trading forbids placing firm or personal trades ahead of client trades. The practice is inconsistent with the Code.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Proprietary priority in the same name is exactly a client-facing trading procedure the Code covers.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — proprietary priority

questions.stem: A marketed composite omits accounts that terminated during the period. Relative to the Code this presentation is most likely:

options.A: Consistent with Performance and Valuation if the remaining accounts were valued at fair market and the composite still has more than five names.
options.B: Consistent because terminated accounts no longer pay fees, so including them would mix non-client results into a client composite. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Inconsistent with Performance and Valuation. Performance must be fair, accurate, and complete; dropping terminated accounts is a classic cherry-pick.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Fair marks on the survivors do not make an incomplete composite complete.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Terminated accounts belong in the history of the composite that actually included them.
rationales.C: Correct. Principle 5 requires complete presentation. Omitting terminated accounts is the inconsistent pattern.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS c — dropped terminated accounts

drills.los_text: recommend practices and procedures designed to prevent violations of the Asset Manager Code
drills.reading_name: Asset Manager Code of Professional Conduct

questions.stem: After an equal-share IPO allocation, the most appropriate recommended procedure is:

options.A: A firm-level control: put the IPO into the allocation engine by mandate, log exceptions, and require compliance sign-off before the allocation is final — not a lecture to one trader to “be fair.”
options.B: Remind the trader who keyed the tickets to use professional judgment next time, and leave the written policy unchanged because the Code is about individual character rather than systems.
options.C: Move the IPO into the proprietary book first going forward, then offer leftover shares to clients who complain, which avoids repeating an even-split across the advisory book. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Correct. Prevention is institutional. Recommend a concrete firm procedure (policy, system, record, sign-off), not a pep talk.
rationales.B: Incorrect. “Remind the analyst to be fair” is not a recommended procedure under this LOS.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Proprietary priority would add a Trading breach rather than prevent one.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — firm procedure not lecture

questions.stem: Which recommendation best prevents Principle 4 failures of the “title-only compliance officer” type?

options.A: Add a second honorary compliance title on the CIO's card so that marketing can show two names without changing reporting lines or halt rights. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Name a compliance officer with authority to restrict trading and escalate to the governing body, and resource surveillance so that officer can actually halt a trade.
options.C: Keep compliance reporting into the trading desk for speed, but require the officer to initial the blotter at the close of each session after fills are complete.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Extra titles without authority do not create a program.
rationales.B: Correct. Minimum prevention: a named officer with real authority and the systems to use it. That is the firm-level control Principle 4 requires.
rationales.C: Incorrect. After-the-fact initials from a desk-reporting officer do not restrict trading in time.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — officer with authority

questions.stem: A private equity line still sits at last-round cost after a down round. The procedure most likely to prevent a repeat valuation breach is:

options.A: Instruct the deal team to “use judgment” on marks, without a written policy, so that valuation remains flexible when information is incomplete.
options.B: Leave cost on the books until exit, and disclose in a footnote that private holdings are carried at cost, which the firm treats as a complete fair-value policy.
options.C: Adopt a fair-value policy with independent input and a stated review calendar for Level-3 / illiquid assets, then apply it when a material event occurs.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Unwritten judgment is not a preventive control.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A cost footnote does not turn stale cost into fair value after a material event.
rationales.C: Correct. Recommend a documented fair-value policy, independent input, and a review calendar — a firm procedure, not a hope that the deal team remembers.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — valuation policy

questions.stem: The desk has a written allocation policy that nobody follows. The most appropriate recommendation is:

options.A: Enforcement authority and testing: sample IPO books and allocation logs, give compliance halt/escalation rights, and fix the procedure when a test fails — not another copy of the same PDF.
options.B: Rewrite the policy in a longer font and recirculate it annually, because a more complete document is the control even if desks ignore it. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Withdraw the written policy so that informal custom, if it happens to be fair this quarter, cannot be accused of diverging from a paper standard.

rationales.A: Correct. If a policy is ignored, the recommendation is authority and testing, not another memo. A written policy that is not followed is already inconsistent with the Code.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Lengthening the PDF does not create enforcement.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Deleting the policy removes the audit trail; it does not install a control.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — enforce ignored policy

questions.stem: Which set of firm procedures is most complete as a prevention package for Asset Manager Code breaches?

options.A: Annual ethics training for analysts only, with no named officer, no allocation engine, and no valuation policy, on the view that trained individuals will not need firm systems. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick. Keep the mechanism, not the slogan, in view when you pick.
options.B: Formal adoption by the governing body; a named officer with authority; written policies covering loyalty, gifts, suitability, fair dealing, best execution, IPO allocation, personal trading, valuation, and performance; timely conflict/fee/risk disclosure with a file; resources and periodic testing.
options.C: A one-page mission statement that the firm “puts clients first,” posted in reception, without records, surveillance, or a review calendar for illiquid marks. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client. Grade the practice by what it actually does for the client.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Individual training is necessary but never sufficient — the Code is a firm code.
rationales.B: Correct. Prevention is institutional: adopt, empower, write the policies the six principles require, disclose, resource, and test.
rationales.C: Incorrect. A slogan without records or surveillance is not a recommended procedure.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — minimum prevention set

questions.stem: A recommended disclosure control that helps prevent Principle 6 breaches is most likely:

options.A: Limit disclosure to the ADV brochure at onboarding, with no follow-up when fees or the investment process change, because onboarding documents are deemed continuing.
options.B: Disclose conflicts only if the related trade was later found to be unfair; fair trades need not be accompanied by conflict disclosure under the Code. The item is testing that operational difference, not a label.
options.C: Disclose conflicts, fees, risks, and material process changes to clients in a timely way, and keep a file of what was disclosed and when, so a client or regulator can reconstruct the communication.

rationales.A: Incorrect. Material changes after onboarding still need timely communication.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Fairness of the trade does not waive the conflict disclosure.
rationales.C: Correct. Timely disclosure plus a file is a concrete firm procedure. Silence about a conflict is a disclosure failure even when the trade was otherwise fair.

questions.curriculum_ref: AMC LOS d — disclosure file
